label: ISS (low Earth orbit)
equipment: Exercise: a resistive device (ARED), a treadmill (T2) and a cycle (CEVIS)
Eye checks: visual acuity testing software, ocular ultrasound, ophthalmic imaging and optical coherence tomography (OCT)
Body mass: SLAMMD (Space Linear Acceleration Mass Measurement Device)
Radiation: dosimeter badges worn by the crew and radiation area monitors
Sleep and activity: a wrist sensor (actigraph) that records movement and light
Medical: a pharmacy and a suite of medical equipment, with ultrasound scans done by the crew
Support: regular contact with flight surgeons, and return to Earth in the crew's own spacecraft in an emergency

label: Lunar surface
equipment: We found no NASA page that lists medical equipment for the lunar surface. The items below are for Orion, the spacecraft that carries crews to the Moon.
Radiation: six radiation sensors in the cabin (HERA), with on-screen warnings and an audible alarm, and active dosimeters worn by the crew
Radiation shelter: built by the crew from stowage bags in the central part of the crew module
Exercise: a compact device NASA described for Orion (ROCKY), used like a rowing machine and for strength training

label: Mars transit
equipment: No Mars transit vehicle exists yet, so there is no equipment list to cite.
NASA says a Mars crew must bring all the food, equipment and medical supplies it needs, with no resupply
NASA expects a communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way, so the crew must solve problems with minimal support from Earth
